thread.title: Gene-Edited Beagles Could Offer Hope to Dog Lovers Who Have Allergies
thread.title_full: Gene-Edited Beagles Could Offer Hope to Dog Lovers Who Have Allergies

author: Renz Soliman
title: Gene-Edited Beagles Could Offer Hope to Dog Lovers Who Have Allergies
text:
Gene-edited beagles that lack a key allergy-triggering protein are offering new hope to people who love dogs but cannot live with them because of medical reasons.
Scientists at New York-based biotech company Kindred Companion Sciences used CRISPR gene-editing technology to create two beagle puppies, Bailey and her twin Alfie, that do not produce Can f 1, the major dog allergen found in saliva, hair and dander.
Researchers first edited the Can f 1 gene in dog skin cells, disrupting the recipe the cells use to make the protein, according to NBC News.
Genetically-Altered Beagles
The edited genetic material was then transferred into eggs and implanted into a surrogate beagle, which gave birth to the two healthy pups in September 2024. Laboratory tests later showed no detectable Can f 1 in the dogs' fur or saliva, while control samples from poodles and goldendoodles contained high levels of the allergen.
To check whether the gene edit actually prevents allergic reactions, scientists performed skin-prick tests on Matt Walker, Kindred's CEO, who has long‑standing dog allergies.
His skin reacted to extracts from conventional breeds, including poodles and goldendoodles, but showed no reaction to saliva and dander from Bailey and Alfie.
Walker has lived with Bailey for more than a year and reports no allergic symptoms, suggesting that removing Can f 1 can meaningfully reduce allergy risk for at least some sufferers. The research, published in The CRISPR Journal, is the first peer‑reviewed study to demonstrate a targeted genetic knockout of the major dog allergen in live dogs.
Kindred says veterinary exams and growth tracking show the beagles are developing normally, with no obvious health or behavioral problems so far. Whole‑genome sequencing did not reveal off‑target edits, indicating that the CRISPR change was confined to the intended gene, GenEng News reported.
Tackling One of Many Dog Allergens
The specific Can f 1 mutation is rare but does occur naturally in some dogs, which Walker and colleagues argue lowers the likelihood of serious long‑term side effects.
However, scientists caution that Can f 1 is only one of several dog allergens, so the approach may not work for every allergy sufferer, and broader clinical data will be needed.
The company is now planning to test the technique in other breeds and service animals to see if it can establish lines of allergy‑reduced dogs beyond beagles.
Any future sale of such pets remains years away: Kindred must continue monitoring Bailey and Alfie's health, scale up breeding in a genetically diverse dog population, and seek approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration before offering gene‑edited dogs to consumers.
For millions of people who currently avoid dogs because of allergies, these beagles mark an early but significant step toward owning pets that are biologically engineered to be easier to live with, as per ABC News.
